agent_notes: The five English versions split on the verb: KJV/Webster 'gave them up', ASV 'let them go', YLT 'send them away', BBE 'gave them up'. I keep the root's plain sense, 'I sent him off', because the Piel of שׁלח is the verb of releasing a slave or driving out, and the commentaries (Radak, Metzudat David) split between 'withdrew my guarding' and 'sent them into exile'. STEPBible's 'and I gave over it' is an artifact of the suffix; the suffix is a masculine singular 'him', Israel as one.
Meiri says singular 'him' with plural 'their heart' is the usual way scripture speaks of the assembly of Israel. I rendered the shift literally and let the dramatic layer smooth it.

Rashi's gloss of שרירות as 'appearance' ties it to שׁוּרָי (Ps 5:9, 'my watchers'); Ibn Ezra ties it to שריר 'firm'. I follow the standard sense 'stubbornness', which also fits Jer 3:17 (my own cross-reference, not from the packet).

STEPBible glosses לוּ as 'if'; in the optative 'if only' use (BDB 'O that') the sense is a wish, not a condition. KJV 'had hearkened' (past) and ASV 'would hearken' (future) are both defensible; the participle שֹׁמֵעַ is tenseless, so I kept it present in the literal layer.

כִּמְעַט is read by Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri and Metzudat David as 'in a little while'. Radak and Meiri explicitly call the כ a true kaph of time ('like a little'). KJV 'I should soon have subdued' is a sound rendering of the conditional that follows from לוּ; the verbs are imperfect and the conditional is implied by v.14. Literal layer keeps the simple future.

agent_notes: יכחשו is the crux: YLT 'feign obedience' is the Piel sense 'to lie, to deny' with ל (Ps 18:45, 66:3 'your enemies shall cringe to you'); KJV 'submitted themselves' is the same idea rendered by its effect. BBE 'broken' loses the verb. I take the subject as the enemies of the LORD, with Radak and Metzudat David. Malbim reads the lying as denying God's existence; I do not follow him. 'Their time' (עתם) is ambiguous between the enemies' doom (Rashi, Malbim) and Israel's time of blessing (Radak, Metzudat David). I keep the Hebrew ambiguity in the literal layer and choose the doom reading in the dramatic layer; flag for the reviewer.

agent_notes: The verb ויאכילהו is formally a wayyiqtol ('and he fed him'); the speaker shifts from third person 'he fed him' to first person 'I satisfy you'. Ibn Ezra and Meiri treat this as the ordinary prophetic alternation of voice, and Meiri reads the wayyiqtol as standing for a future. The English versions all render it as a conditional 'would feed', dependent on v.14. I keep the Hebrew's own shifts in the literal layer and treat the whole as conditional on v.14; whether 'he' is God or the enemy-subject of v.16 is argued by Ibn Ezra (who says 'all the commentators' take it as God, with Israel as the object).

agent_notes: The speaker shifts mid-verse from the psalmist to a voice the psalmist 'hears' (שפת לא ידעתי אשמע). Who 'I' is, and whose language it is, is disputed: Joseph hearing Egyptian (Rashi, Metzudat David via Sotah 36b), Israel hearing Egyptian, or the psalmist hearing an unfamiliar divine voice (Malbim). I translate the Hebrew as it stands and keep both readings open in the commentary. I could not source the claim that the form יהוסף is a deliberate honorific longer spelling beyond Ibn Ezra's own remark, which I cite.
